blocks.text: Huygens' principle, first stated by the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens, is a geometrical method for finding the shape of a wavefront at a later time from its known shape at some instant. Huygens assumed that every point of a wavefront can be considered a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in all directions with a speed equal to the speed of the wave. The new wavefront at a later time is the surface tangent to all the secondary wavelets, called their envelope.

In Fig 15.2 the wavefront AB moves outward from a source S. To find its shape after a time t, assume the wave speed v is the same everywhere, so in time t the wave travels a distance vt. Draw circles (traces of spherical wavelets) of radius vt centred on points along AB. The envelope of these wavelets, the curve CD, is the new wavefront. All the results of Huygens' principle can also be obtained from Maxwell's equations, but Huygens' simple model is easier to use.

blocks.alt: A source S at the left. A blue arc AB is the present wavefront, with dots marking points on it. From each dot a grey arc of radius vt is drawn. A red arc CD touches the outer edges of all the grey arcs: it is the new wavefront after time t. An arrow labelled vt joins AB to CD.
blocks.caption: Huygens' construction of a new wavefront (original diagram after Fig 15.2).
blocks.long_description: Each point of the old wavefront acts like a tiny new source. After time t all the tiny wavelets have the same radius vt, and the surface that just touches them all is where the wave has reached.

blocks.prompt: Can Huygens' principle be applied to sound and water waves?
blocks.explanation: Yes. It applies to any wave travelling at a definite speed, so it explains the spreading and bending of sound and water waves as well as light.

items: Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets.
New wavefront = envelope of the wavelets after time t (radius vt).
